items.summary: Scientists found that caffeine activates an ancient cellular energy system involved in stress resistance, DNA repair, and growth. The discovery could help explain caffeine’s links to healthier aging and may point toward new ways to target the same pathway.

items.title: Searching for unknown fungi in the Norwegian mountains
items.summary: During some days in August, science takes center stage. The experts are surveying the little-known diversity of fungi found in the alpine Dryas heath. They may even discover species that have never been described scientifically before.

items.title: One of the oldest known 3D animal fossils found in Norwegian sheep field
items.summary: One of the oldest known 3D fossils of an animal has been discovered in a sheep field in the Norwegian Arctic, the first new major site of its kind anywhere in Europe in decades.

items.title: Action on climate and air pollution likely to boost economy, UN says
items.summary: Every US$1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together can generate around US$15 in economic benefits, according to a report published today by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC).

items.title: Germany's 15-year-olds post lowest PISA results since testing began 25 years ago
items.summary: The PISA study regularly assesses 15-year-olds' ability to understand and solve real-life problems in reading, mathematics and science toward the end of their compulsory education. items.title: Researchers rewire ribosomes to specialize in one protein
items.summary: Every cell relies on ribosomes, the molecular machines that read genetic instructions and use them to assemble proteins. A cell needs thousands of types of proteins at any one time, so ribosomes must be generalists, capable of using instructions to produce any protein.

items.title: When disaster strikes, what happens to our pets?
items.summary: As large-scale disasters—including earthquakes, torrential rains, typhoons and wildfires—become increasingly frequent, ensuring that pets as well as their owners can evacuate safely and receive appropriate care has become an important part of disaster preparedness.

items.title: Tiny molecular rings open new ways for designing better medicines
items.summary: Cyclopropanes are organic chemistry's smallest rings. Three carbon atoms are joined in a triangle, creating a compact and unusually strained structure. items.title: Prehistoric builders hauled 25-tonne stones at least 18 km to build iconic Devil's Arrows
items.summary: New research has revealed that ancient builders deliberately transported enormous 25-tonne stones across at least 18 kilometers (11 miles) to build Britain's tallest surviving prehistoric stone row—the iconic Devil's Arrows.

items.title: Untangling the meta-biomaterial puzzle one property at a time
items.summary: From repairing damaged tissues to developing better implants, many medical developments depend on materials that can mimic the complex properties of human tissue. items.title: A new mission could rendezvous with Halley's Comet in 2061
items.summary: Halley's Comet captures the imagination in a way that few other astronomical objects do. items.title: Grandchildren repay childhood care by supporting ailing grandparents in Hong Kong
items.summary: As Hong Kong Special Administrative Region's population ages at one of the fastest rates in the world, demand for family elder care increases daily. items.title: NASA technique for manipulating satellite photos now reveals ancient images
items.summary: High in the central tower of Angkor Wat, an ancient Cambodian temple, paintings depict horseback riders and a traditional musical ensemble. Thousands of visitors pass these images daily without noticing them because they are faded to the point of invisibility.

items.title: Helium-3 lifts new quantum computing concept with faster tunneling rates
items.summary: Helium—the lightest atom that can be laser-cooled and controlled—powers a new design for high-powered, stable quantum computers.

items.title: A crystalline sponge reveals structures of large 'beyond rule of 5' molecules
items.summary: Drug discovery has traditionally followed the "rule of 5," which identifies chemical properties generally associated with good absorption of orally administered drugs, including a molecular weight below 500 daltons (Da). items.title: No evidence that Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs have improved child protection outcomes
items.summary: New research concludes that Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs (MASHs) are failing to provide better protection for children in England, instead causing families distress and putting more pressure on social care resources.

items.title: Not all eggs are the same—uncovering a tropical parasite's secret weapons
items.summary: A team of scientists from the Faculty of Science at Charles University has achieved a major breakthrough in research into schistosomiasis, a serious tropical disease affecting more than 250 million people worldwide. items.summary: Jaden Caradine knew he wanted to be an engineer at eight years old. He just took a winding road to get there. items.summary: Nanographenes can be considered molecular fragments of graphene, a 2D conductive material in which carbon atoms are connected in a honeycomb pattern. items.summary: We can all see the huge waste of talent this represents for the young people concerned and society as a whole.

items.title: NASA Calls for Proposals to Accelerate Lunar Surface Technologies
items.summary: NASA is seeking proposals to advance the technology and infrastructure needed to explore the Moon and establish a Moon Base in the lunar South Pole region. Announced on Tuesday, Sept. 8, the solicitation targets capability gaps, including power generation, oxygen extraction, and producing materials
